At the time I had received an intimation which I understood to imply that it was compound interest.

That it was simple
interest.

Yes, that is quite right; I understand the auditor to say that it was computed on the basis of simple interest. I have seen the auditor since, and I find that I misunderstood his intimation to me, and that it is compound interest. There were no instructions given to the auditor at all. The statute was before him when he made the calculation, and the auditor determined upon his own judgment absolutely that the statute called for a compound interest calculation. I do not want to act as judge upon this point, but I wish to say that the hon. member for St. John quite overstated the matter when he said that the statute was very clear that no compound interest should be charged. Certainly, the country has to pay compound interest upon it; certainly the least to be said is that one would have thought that it would be called for. It seems, upon reading the section, that if anything the view of the auditor is better than that of the hon. member for St. John. How does the section read?
The expression "cost of construction," in the case of the eastern division, shall mean and include all the cost of material, supplies, wages, services and transportation, etc.... cost of engineering, maintenance, repairs and replace-

ment of works and material during- construction, and superintendence, bookkeeping, legal expenses, and, generally, costs and expenses occasioned by the construction of the said division, whether of the same kind as, or different in kind from, the classes of expenditure specially mentioned, including interest upon the money expended ;-
That is to say, that in the outlay of any year, the interest outlay of that year is a part of the cost of construction. I will ask the hon. member to remember that.
-the interest upon such outlay-
Which means the interest upon the annual outlay, including interest-
-the interest upon such outlay in each year shall be capitalized at the end of such year, and interest charged thereon at three per cent per annum until the completion of the work, and until the lessees enter into possession under the terms of the said lease.
It is a question of what the word " out-_ lay " means, and if " outlay " means, as a reasonable interpretation would say, the cost of construction during the year before, then certainly it is compound interest. If it means the same as the "cost of construction" of the year before then it is compound and it can be nothing else, because, in the course of construction, the interest payment of that year is included. So that it would mean the interest upon (x plus y) all payments for other purposes and all payments for interest.

It is added to the outlay in that year, of course, and then at the end of the year that represents the expenditure of that year. The Act says it shall bear interest at three per cent until the completion of the line, but not that that interest shall be compounded each year as has been done here.
If interest shall include interest outlay during the year, then it includes the interest upon outlay during the year, and, consequently, interest upon outlay means interest upon interest outlay.

True it is the interest
for that year which is added, but then the statute goes on and says that that total outlay for that year including the interest shall only bear interest at three per cent until the road is completed. Suppose a man gives a note of $1,000 payable in ten years at 6 per cent, you cannot compound up that interest every year, but at the end of the period you get your principal amount and the interest at 6 per cent.

If, on the other hand, it	says	tnat interest in	eachyear	shall	be	part of	outlay,	and
that interest shall be capitalized at the end of the year, that means compound interest. However, I am not arguing that there is no other view reasonably tenable; I am only arguing that the auditors had very good ground for their view, and in my humble judgment they have the better ground of the two. The auditors followed this view and took this course upon their reading of the Act, and askeu for no opinion upon it.
What is the legal opinion of the Solicitor General?

My own opinion is that the auditors' view is more reasonable than that of the hon. member for St. John. I am not in the habit of deciding things and saying there is no possible other view at all; I am not of that habit especially when I possessed just a few years ago an entirely different opinion, and that is the position the hon. member for St. John is in to-night.
Not at all.

Oh, yes. He argued tonight that the question of location is as much a matter for the Grand Trunk as for us, when he knows that his Government acted upon the very opposite opinion given by the Minister of Justice of that day.
I know they did not. When the location is once agreed upon and the specifications based on it, that is the end of it.
The question of location, according to his own Minister of Justice, never had to be agreed upon.

What has placing the workshops nine miles away from the line of the Transcontinental and buying a road from another company, got to do with the location of the line? Is not that changing the whole character of the terminals so far as the workshops are concerned?

It is changing the location, that is all; changing that portion of its character, but nothing else, and that is something within the purview of the Government alone, and has always been held to be.
What I am now about to say does not concern the issue, but I promised the hon. member from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that

I would call attention to his own words and appeal to the House as to whether I did not properly represent him. To do so, I will read the statement that preceded the remarks of the hon. member. Some discussion ensued between him and the Minister of Militia as to certain allegations which on certain information the hon. gentleman from St. John had made, and this took place:
Major General Hughes:	The hon. gentleman
has not the slightest particle of evidence that there is a tittle of fact in what he has stated, and he cannot produce any. He cannot show that the British Government in Britain, in Canada, in the United States, or in any other part of God's green universe, ever was able to get mark vii ammunition at less than $35 a thousand, excepting the one lot that I had the honour of being instrumental in getting for $33 per thousand.
Mr. Pugsley:	My hon. friend may be absolutely correct. I have not the slightest idea as to whether I am correct or not. It may be that the gentleman who gave me this information gave me false information.
Is not that just about what I said? And so we see from this that the hon. gentleman took upon himself to impugn the honour of the Government upon information which he had not the slightest idea was correct or not.
I do not think the hon. member is right in saying that I impugned the honour of the Government.
The hon. gentleman said that it involved the honour of the Government.

I was careful to state that I did not make any charge against the Government. I was careful to state I had received this information in New York from a gentleman in whose word I placed confidence, a gentleman of the highest respectability; but that, so far as I was concerned, I did not know whether the statement were correct. I was careful to say I made no charge against the Government or against the minister.

What, in the opinion of the Solicitor General, is the meaning of the word " railway " in line 7 of section 7 of the contract? The hon. gentleman has told us that the word " work " means the whole railway. What would be the definition of the word " railway "; would it be the same definition as is contained in the general Railway Act?

I do not think the general Railway Act applies at all. I say . 117
that the word " railway " has no definition in this Act, and that is the complaint I make. What the hon. gentleman asks me to do now is to fill up the blank in the Act, which the Government he supported should have filled up by direct legislation.
As a member of the House I was asking the Solicitor General what in his opinion was the meaning of the word " railway."

I do not know that I should be called upon across the floor to give a definition of " railway " or any other thing. What I say is that the definition of " railway " and of " completed railway " should have been made in the Act itself, beyond all peradventure.
It was.
It was not made as to " completed railway."
Yes.
Where is the definition?
I will tell you.

There is no definition of a completed railway or what constitutes the completeness of a railway, and that is the point my hon. friend (Mr. Devlin) has in mind. What constitutes the completion of a railway is not defined in this legislation, and it ought to have been.

The point is, what is really the meaning of the word " railway." Section 7 says:
The work must be under the joint supervision, inspection and acceptance of the chief engineer appointed by the Government and the chief engineer of the company.
The Solicitor General says the word "work" means the whole railway, and I now ask him the definition of the word "railway"?
Mr. MEIGHEN That is to say, is the railway complete until there are shops and the like of that?

I am not asking that; I am asking the Solicitor General for .a definition of the word "railway" as he understands it in this contract; it must have some meaning.
Mr. MEIGHEN; I do not propose to commit myself to a definition, because, in the first place, it would do no good to do so. There was a time when it would do good, and that time was



overlooked by the Government which the hon. gentleman supported. It will now have to be submitted to another tribunal.

Would the Solicitor General say, as Solicitor General, that the word "railway" would not mean:
"Any railway which the company had authority to construct or operate, including all branches, sidings, stations, depots, wharves, rolling stock, equipment, stores, property real and personal, and works connected therewith, and also any railways, bridges, tunnels or other structure which the company is authorized to construct."

That is so easy that I really cannot help answering it. In my opinion, "work" does not include rolling stock at all, because we have nothing to do with rolling stock; the company has to supply that. The hon. gentleman's definition is wrong, whatever other definition may be right.
Would it mean all the stations of the road?
It would mean stations of the railway, of course. It might not mean all the stations.
Would not the terminal stations be the stations of the railway?
They might and they might not. That is to be decided.
What the hon. gentleman is driving at is this: there is a station for the company to go into at Quebec just as there is at Winnipeg.

I shall be very brief in explaining to my hon. friend why I think the Grand Trunk Pacific were willing, when Mr. Hays was living, and would be willing to-day, to make the arrangement about which I spoke. The result would be, to begin with, that they would get their operating expenses. Then they would be developing traffic which in the future would be for the benefit of the country served by that railway. While operating, they would be at the same time postponing the period when they would be obliged to begin to pay interest. My hon. friend must see that. Therefore it would be very much more favourable for the company to take sections, and even the whole line before it was finally completed than it would be to enter into a lease under which their obligations to pay rent would begin at a certain time. The company might be willing to make the

arrangement of which I spoke and which they expressed themselves formerly as willing to make, while they would not be willing to enter into a lease for an uncompleted road, under which, as I have said, the term for payment of interest would begin to run. The best way to find out is to ask them if they are now willing to carry out the proposed agreement.

The discussion so far has been in regard to the eastern end of the Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise. It strikes me that the western end is more important, and I wish to call the attention of the House for a few minutesi to the effect of action that may be taken under this resolution. The resolution contemplates the taking over by the Government of the portion of the Grand Trunk Pacific line from Lake Superior junction to Fort William, with the terminals. That piece of line is necessary to give the Grand Trunk Pacific system, measurably gridironing the three prairie provinces and British Columbia, a competitive outlet to lake navigation. If the Government takes action under this resolution and deprives the Grand Trunk Pacific of that access to lake navigation, it will be prejudicing in large measure the operations of the company throughout the three prairie provinces and British Columbia.
But they would have to get connection from Winnipeg to Lake Superior junction, supposing the arrangement were carried out. They would need to enter into a contract for that.

Yes. I will reach the point that my hon. friend has in mind a little later on.
At the present time the Grand Trunk Pacific has a railway system in large measure covering the four western provinces, which system is dependent for its commercial success, in larger measure than on any o.theT factor, on having independent access on competitive terms to the navigation of the Great Lakes. They have that connection now under some arrangement-I do not know what it is- with the Government, covering that part of the line from Winnipeg to Lake Superior junction, and then by the use oi this brandh which is- their own. I am compelled to understand, from the terms of this resolution, and more particularly from the expressions of the Solicitor General in regard to it, that it is the deliberate intention of the Government under this legislation to deprive the Grand

Trunk Pacific system of that access to lake Superior, which is an absolute necessity to its successful business operation. The Government proposes to take over this section of the line, which is the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific, with its terminals, with the elevators, with all the port facilities which have 'been established there by the Grand Trunk Pacific at the cost of that railway, to aid in the successful operation of those thousands of miles of line in the Prairie Provinces and the Pacific province. I do not imagine that the House understands the stupendous character of the proposal before it. My hon. friend the Solicitor General, if I heard him correctly, spoke of the necessity, by this legislation, of taking over the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific-of expropriating-
No, I did not.
The hon. member used the word "expropriate."

Yes, I did; but the hon. member has never been unfair to me before, and he does not mean to be now. What I said was that if we had to operate the road, then we had to lease or acquire, and that we desired the power to acquire, because it might otherwise be impossible for us to make an advantageous lease.
Exactly. My hon. friend used the word "expropriate" and also the word "weapon." The Government proposes to use this as a weapon in dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Why should it not?
I understand there is an intention on the part of the Government to use this agreement as a weapon to do what?
To get a fair bargain.
As a weapon to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to submit to a rearrangement of their agreement in regard to the eastern division of the Transcontinental.
No.

That is the only purpose there could be in using this arrangement as a weapon. I am not interested particularly in whether or not the Government takes the Grand Trunk Pacific by the throat and uses this agreement as a weapon to deprive it of the possibility of operating properly its system in the prairie provinces and the Pacific province. That 1171
is a matter of Government policy; and, if the Government sees fit to adopt that policy, that is for the Government to consider. What I am interested in is this: the Grand Trunk Pacific project was begun for the especial purpose of giving Western Canada railway development and railway competition, And my hon. friends propose by this means to take into their hands the power to deprive the Prairie Provinces and British Columbia of the possibility of their enjoying that competition in railway facilities that was the purpose of the establishment of the enterprise. If the Government of the day actually does as they have taken power to do, how is the Grand Trunk Pacific to carry on its business as a competitor with the other two railway systems of the West, both of which not only have access to the waters of Lake Superior, but also have, or shortly will have, all-rail connection with the East? If they 'take the control they have arranged to take here, they break, the Grand-Trunk Pacific enterprise; and that, I -am bound to believe,-is their deliberate intention. As to the use of the Bill to be founded upon this resolution as a weapon to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to enter into an agreement as to operating the eastern section of the railway on unfair terms-
It is not that at all.
My hon. friend will have to admit that, or he used the word inadvisedly.

The hon. gentleman is misquoting me. I said not to affect in any way the operating of the eastern division. If they are ready to operate the eastern division, we are only too ready to let them. If they refuse to operate, where is their eastern outlet that my hon. friend is ' so much afraid of?

I do not think it would be profitable for my hon. friend and myself to argue about the meaning of the terms he used. There is no question about the use of the term; there is no question about the connection in which he used it. I am, therefore, entitled to put my construction upon the purpose he had in the use of these terms, as he is at liberty to put such construction on what I say.
So long as you quote correctly what I said.

And the hon. gentleman will not deny-he cannot deny, for Hansard

will show it-that he used the word " expropriate," and the word " weapon."
Hear, hear; but not in the way the hon. gentleman says I did.
That is the matter that I say it is not profitable for my hon. friend and myself to discuss.
Who owns it now?
Owns what now?
The property to be expropriated?

The Grand Trunk Pacific. It is important that there should be railway competition, and that there should be a competitive outlet for the Grand Trunk Pacific system, not only to the Lakes, but also to tidewater; and it is in regard to the terms upon which the Grand
11 p.m. Trunk Pacific shall secure access to tidewater that this resolution is brought forward-as my hon. friend says-as a "weapon" to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific-he did not use the word "compel"; I am using it-to agree to something that the Government is not entitled, on the merits of the case, to require them to agree to. Now, as to the right of the Government to claim breach of faith on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific-and that is really the burden of my hon. friend's argument-as to the merits of the case between the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific concerning the eastern outlet at tidewater, let me give my view of the case concerning where the responsibility rests.
The Grand Trunk Pacific project was finally agreed to in April, 1904. From 1904 until 1911 construction was pushed on that road. In October, 1911, if my memory is correct, a return, placed on the table of the House by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, gave the information that at that time an expenditure of approximately $100,000,000 had been made, and that the road was within, I think, 15 per cent of being completed-it was 85 per cent completed. Details were given showing so much grading, bridging, track laying and other things to be done. The cost had been $100,000,000, approximately, and the time occupied from the very beginning of the enterprise was seven years.
I have never seen that return.

The return was laid on the table, and there was a long argument in Parliament about it. The return was
CMr. Oliver.]
brought down and the figures given, for the purpose of affecting the election in South Renfrew, which resulted in the return of my hon. friend (Mr. Graham).
I would like to see my hon. friend produce that return.
My hon. friend surely does not deny that he brought down a return.
I do not think I ever brought down a return showing an expenditure of $100,000,000 at that time.
Was the expenditure less or more?
It was more.
How much more?
I am not prepared to say.

I may be wrong as to the amount. But for the purposes of the argument I am going to make it would be better if the amount were larger than $100,000,000. Now, let me repeat in seven years the road was 85 per cent completed, and the cost was approximately a hundred millions.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the return stated that it was 85 per cent completed?
That is my understanding of the return.
I think the hon. gentleman will have to revise that understanding.

Perhaps so. I give the figures as approximate and may be a little in error, but approximately, that was the condition. Now, it is three and a half years since 1911, and the expenditure on the Transcontinental has gone up to something like-should I be wrong if I said, $150,000,000?
Oh, oh.
Has it gone over that?
Does the hon. gentleman include interest?
I include anything the hon. gentleman includes. I take it any way he figures it. How does he figure it out?
That depends on the basis on which the hon. gentleman wishes it figured out. Does he include interest?
Yes, anything the hon. gentleman likes.
The expenditure is over $170,000,000.

We will say it was $170,000,000 at December 31, 1914, and that it was $105,000,000 or $110 000,000 at the 1st of October, 1911-and it was no more than that. The road was 85 per cent completed then, and it is not completed yet.
It was not 85 per cent completed then.
I said it was. I may be a little in error. Will my hon. friend say how much it was?
It was not nearly that. The hon. gentleman's figures show it was not nearly that.
The hon. member for South Renfrew put it at 55 per cent last year in the discussion of the' Transcontinental-55 per cent completed when this Government took office.

I do not know what the
hon. member for South Renfrew said.

Neither does the hon.
member.

I am taking the return
submitted by the Minister of Railways when the hon. member for South Renfrew was not in the House. What I wanted to say was that the railway was certainly more than 75 per cent completed in the fall of 1911, and since that time this Government has spent upon the railroad more than one-half as much as was spent in the seven years previously, and if the railroad is not completed now, it is the fault of this Government, which has squandered money in such stupendous volume without putting it to proper use. If the Goverment of the day had spent the money which they have spent as the Government which preceded them spent the money, that they spent, there would be no dispute to-day as to whether or not the Transcontinental was ready for operation, The Grand Trunk Pacific would not have a leg to stand on in arguing that they were under no obligation to take over the road. My hon. friend would not be in the position that, by an Act of this Parliament, he must take the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific to use it as a weapon to compel the company to agree to take over the road when it has not been completed. There is no reason why this Transcontinental railroad is not completed at this date,
except the policy of the Government of the day.
Who let the contracts for the road?
The late Government did not let any contracts for the changes in Quebec.

I know you did not,
and you did not do any work there; that is more.

It does not make any difference who let the contracts. Now that my hon. friend has mentioned it all the contracts were let before the present Government came into power, and if they did not see that these contracts were fulfilled as they ought to have been, it was not the fault of the Government that let the contracts.

The contracts in
Quebec were let to be finished in 1907, and they were not finished when we came into power.
That is right, they are not finished yet, so that my hon. friend is not gaining anything in the race at all.

That may be your
opinion.

The fact that the road is not completed to-day is not because there has not been time enough or because there has not been money enough spent, but because it has not been the policy of this Government to carry that project to successful and satisfactory completion. It has been the settled and fixed policy of this Government to prevent the realization of the expectations of railroad competition throughout Canada, and particularly throughout Western Canada, as the result of the completion of the Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise, that was the very reason for its inception. That is absolutely in line with the policy of the hon. gentlemen opposite from the day that the project was first brought into Parliament. They opposed it in 1903 and in 1904 they fought the project until the snow flew in October-from spring until fall. From that day to this they have done everything in season and out of season, by word of mouth but still more by executive action, to prevent the successful completion of this project and the realization of the expectations resulting from it. Here we have the climax. The rails are laid from end to end of the road. There is no reason

why the terminals should not have progressed as the building of the road progressed; but we find the road laid and the terminals still to be built and our hon. friends contend that the company should take over the road without the terminals being completed! The Minister of Railways says: Why, they can get down to tide water, they can use the Canadian Pacific railway station, they can transact their business. My friend the Solicitor General was very sarcastic about the amount of business there was for them to transact. Perhaps there is not very much business for them to transact, perhaps they could transact their business under the circumstances that exist at the present time. But I ask my hon. friend if he expects that a company that raises as many millions of dollars of capital for expenditure in this country as the Grand Trunk Pacific has done, is going to enter into an agreement that makes it responsible for large payments in regard to its enterprise, if the terms of the agreement have not been completed in regard to terminals and the company is expected to transact its business with such facilities as are offered to it at Quebec today. I say no, that is not reasonable.
So that there may be no question as to what the condition of the railroad was as to completion on the 31st of December, 1911, I would cite the return submitted to Parliament by the Minister of Railways as follows:
Recapitulation: Length, 1,804.7 iniles froan Moncton to Winnipeg.
Grading completed, 1,587.7 miles, or 76 per cent in 21 contracts.
Track laid, 1,378.7 miles and 278 miles in sidings.
Telegraph lines, 892 iniles.
Bridges, 82 per cent.
That was the condition of construction at that time.
It is a long way from 85 per cent.
But it is more than 75 per cent.
And that only covers part of the railway.

I do not know. My hon. friend will have to settle that with the Minister of Railways, who saw fit to lay on the table of the House a certain statement in regard to the construction of that railroad.
I have given the House the figures, and my argument is that, taking over the road in that state of completion, the Government has not used due diligence in the years that
I Mr. Oliver.]
have followed in the matter of the expenditures they have made; and if there is a question to-day as to the (Grand Trunk Pacific taking the road over, the fault lies with this Government in carrying on its policy of hostility to the Grand Trunk Pacific projiect, and hostility to the principle of railway competition in Western Canada.
One of the last contracts on the line to be finished was the Grand Trunk Pacific.
My hon. friend is complaining about what occurred under his own Administration.
Oh no.

The Government must
shoulder responsibility for its own administration. We are charged with having been responsible for the past expenditure on the Grand Trunk Pacific. Are we to be also charged with the delay in its completion? I say that we are not chargeable either for the large expenditure that has taken place'under the hon. minister, or for the delay in the completion of the work. The Government is surely a government that is responsible for what it-does. Surely the men who went out of office in 1911 are not responsible for what the Government of the day is doing in 1915. I say that this proposed legislation is simply carrying out the policy that has been uniformly followed by the party now in power from the inception of this enterprise to the present-a policy of hostility to the success of the enterprise and hostility to the principle of railway competition in Western Canada.

In introducing the resolution I understood the Minister of Railways to say that it was introduced for the purpose of authorizing the Government to operate the road from Winnipeg to Quebec. I find nothing at all in this resolution to that effect. This resolution applies simply to the acquisition of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway from Fort William to Superior Junction. There is nothing at all about operating the road.

Perhaps I did not
express myself very clearly. The object is to operate more effectually the whole system. If we were shut off from operating between Fort Willliam and Superior Junction it would be very bad as we should be shut off from getting to the water and during navigation, we should have to haul the wheat by rail all the way. The idea

is to pay for the operation out of consolidated revenue.

I only want
to understand exactly where we are. What is the ultimate object of the Government I do not know, but I see that they intend to operate the road. So far so good, or rather so bad. But this resolution is simply to authorize the Government to acquire what now belongs to the Grand Trunk Pacific from Fort William to Superior Junction.
The right hon. gentleman will recall that almost exactly a year ago power was given to the Government to operate the Transcontinental. This only enables us more effectually to operate it.

That is on the statute
book now?
Yes.
I understand where we are now. Do the words " or otherwise acquire " in the resolution cover expropriation if that may be necessary?

I think they are wide
enough to include that. We might acquire it without expropriation, of course, were it necessary to acquire it at all.

What is the
meaning of " or of any other company ?

That applies to "terminal facilities	and	accommodation
works." The words are meant to cover the event of such terminal facilities or accommodation works not being under the direct title of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, but of a subsidiary company.

What works
of any other company are intended to be covered by these words?

I am not quite sure just what works the term	accommodation
works" covers, but that is the phrase usually used in connection with a railway. It is necessary to use those words, I think, in order to get the full effect. The words are in the statutes, and consequently have a judicial meaning. They would mean whatever the court has hitherto decided they do mean. That is what they would mean in this legislation. I presume it would include stations.
That is very vague. I have been a pretty long time in Parliament, but this is the first time I have heard of "accommodation works.
Probably repair shops would be included.
Belonging to whom?
Either to the Grand Trunk Pacific, or they may have them under the title of a subsidiary company.

We want to be all straight, so that the next time we have a discussion of this question we shall have the figures right. The Minister of Railways insisted that over $100,000,000 had been expended up to the time this Government came into power. I have the figures before me, and if the minister will look up the figures down to March 17, 1911, he will see that it is very much under $100,000,000.
About $95,000,000, but then there was the expenditure of about eight months more to be added to that.

The minister said it was much over $100,000,000, but this statement shows that the figures given by my hon. friend Mr. Oliver to-night are approximately correct. After that there was about $50,000,000 expended.
The statement in Hansard says $113,000,000.
We only gave a statement of what was actually paid out. My hon. friend owed a great deal of money.
I am taking the figures given to-night. There is a statement here, made by Mr. Bell, I suppose.

We figured that proportioned over the year it would be about $113,000,000. As the minister has pointed out we have had to pay off millions that the late Government owed, and there are millions under litigation to-day, which we cannot avoid, but as to the disposal of which or including it in the cost of constitution the agreement is silent.
The amounts that you are obligated to pay are not in this statement at all.

I know that, but it is surely unfair to argue that we have expended on the road since the difference between that and the amount now expended. The hon. gentlemen became obligated to pay out a certain sum of money but they had not paid it.
The same argument would apply to my 'hon. friend. This Government is obligated to payments that they have not yet paid, and these payments will come in another statement as well.
And they do not include interest.

We were not discussing interest; that is a small matter. My hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) was justified in approximating these figures on the statement which he had in his hand. If we cannot depend on statements coming from the Government, as we found to-night we could not, how are we to make our calculations?

The statements are absolutely right. I thought that what the hon. member for Edmonton was trying to present was so absurd that it would not appeal to the hon. member for Renfrew. The former Government paid out $113,000,000, but they were obligated to pay large sums in addition which were not settled but which were in dispute. The interest was not included, but the hon. member for Edmonton includes interest in one case and forgets to include it in the other.
You left it for my hon. friend to put in interest or leave it out, and he put it in.
I put it in at one end. but I put it in at the other also, and the hon. gentleman should have done the same.
If this statement is correct, it does appeal to the hon. member for Renfrew and substantiates my hon. friend from Edmonton absolutely in what he' said.

What is meant by this:
For all the purposes of section 9 of the said Act, may provide, by purchase, lease or otherwise, rolling stock and equipment, and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and such other company, shall each be authorized on its part to deal accordingly with the said line of railway or terminal facilities and accommodation works as the case may be.

Section 9 of the old Act reads as follows:
The construction of the eastern division and the operation thereof until completed and leased to the company pursuant to the provisions of the agreement shall be under the charge and control of three commissioners, to be appointed by the Governor in Council.

It will be observed that the clause gives power to the Commission during construction to operate. Last year section 9 was amended, the amendment giving the minister power to operate the road not only during construction but until actually leased and taken over. That is the condition of section 9 now. Therefore, the resolution reads that to fulfil these requirements he may purchase whatever rolling stock may be necessary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That subsections 2, 3, 4, 6 and 6 of section 361 of the Railway Act, and section 29, chapter 122 of the statutes of 1903, shall not apply to any such lease or to anything done under the preceding provision.
That means that they shall not be referred to the Board of Railway Commissioners or approved by them.
Yes, it relieves the Government of the necessity, when making this lease with the company, of having the lease approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners.
There is a reference to section 29, of chapter 122, of the statutes of 1903.
That means that you cannot amalgamate with another company.

Section 29, chapter 122,
3 Edward VII, is the section of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company incorporation charter which provides the terms under which they may enter into an amalgamation or lease. This section corresponds to section 361 of the Railway Act, and in order to carry out the effect of the exception as to the applicability of subsections 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the section, we have also to except section 29.
You give the companies the power to amalgamate under these conditions?
The Act does.

I want to say one further word in line with what I said before. In so far as the operations of the main line of the transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Quebec is concerned, the Government built that line under an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and if they cannot come to an understanding with the Grand Trunk Pacific as to-the operation of it, I would certainly think they had a right to withhold it from the

Grand Trunk Pacific and to operate it in any way they please. But I want to point out that the Grand Trunk Pacific have built this section of 150 or 200 miles from Superior junction to Fort William, they have established terminals at Fort William at enormous expense, and they have done this in the full expectation that they were to have the use temporarily of the main line from Winnipeg to Superior junction, so that they could carry on their business until such time as the line from Quebec to Moncton was finished.
There is nothing in the Act to say that.

There is nothing in the Act; I quite appreciate that; but I am talking of this as a business proposition. The Grand Trunk Pacific built that line and went to the expense with that belief and that understanding, and this Government are deliberately undertaking to take from the Grand Trunk Pacific that property which they paid for with the moneys of their bondholders for the purpose of contributing to the success of their main enterprise. There is only one word for that action, and that word is robbery-robbery not in the public interest, but in the interest of the policy of this Government, in the interest of monopoly in transportation.	*

I would not speak to-night were it not for the strong language used by my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), and used, though in a milder form, by other hon. gentlemen on his side of the House. We were told to-night that the Transcontinental railway was of national interest to the people of Canada when my right hon. friend introduced the Bill for its construction in 1903, and that that national interest has grown day by day from that hour to the present, by reason of the fact that the Government, as representing the people, have invested an enormous sum of money in the construction of this railway. In the judgment of the Government engineer, the railway is now completed, and the time has arrived when the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should carry out the terms of the contract it made with the Government in 1904, and operate the railway. I shall not discuss the details of the cost of this railway, nor shall I enter into various other questions which have been raised to-night, but I do want to correct, a false impression which seems to exist in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite as to the attitude of this Government towards
the Transcontinental railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. I am sure my right hon. friend, and every member on his side of the House, will agree with me that no Government could have adopted a child such as we adopted, in the form of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental, and have been more loyal to it than we have been since we came to power. We are loyal to it by reason of the fact that the Canadian people, whom we represent in this Parliament, have such a large investment in that great undertaking, and we believe that the day has now come when the company should carry out its bargain and operate the line from Winnipeg to Moncton. We feel that in the interests of the people of Canada we must press upon the company to carry out their contract, which up to the present they have failed to do. The Grand Trunk Pacific line from Superior Junction to Fort William and Port Arthur is an essential link in the chain of the Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Moncton, and it is inseparably connected with that enterprise. The purpose of the resolution we are now considering is to take power, so that in the event of the Grand Trunk Pacific failing to carry out its agreement we can operate in some form or other that particular link in the chain, which, as I have said, is so essential to the success of the entire scheme.
Let me say most emphatically that it is not the intention of the Government, nor will it be the policy of the Government, to in any way hamper the trade of Western Canada by any action we may take under this resolution. Neither is it the purpose nor desire of the Government to in any way hamper the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific or to in any way interfere with any vested right, or with any interest they have, so long as they deal fairly, and I am satisfied from what I know of the President of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, that the company is disposed to deal fairly. In view of all that has taken place, in view of the enormous cost of the railway,-and I shall not enter now into the question as to who is to blame for that,-while consideration should be given to the objections of the Grand Trunk Railway, there can be no question about the advisability of providing for the operation of this particular line at the present time. The purpose of this resolution is only to ensure that if the Government is obliged to operate the whole line as it is now completed, the Government shall have the necessary power to be able to operate the line from Superior Junction to

Fort William. In so doing, it is not our desire to injure in any way, or to hamper in any way, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Railway Company. It is not correct for hon. gentlemen to say that we bring forward this resolution with a view to hostile action against the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk. The Government have no such thought, and I can assure the House and the country that the Government will continue in the future as in the past to treat this enterprise the same as it has treated all other enterprises, namely, in a spirit of fairness and generosity, which will be creditable to the Government and satisfactory to the people of the Dominion.

I must congratulate the
Government on the statement made by the Minister of Public Works. He will, of course, understand that if we have been led into error it was by reason of the expressions used by his colleague, the Solicitor General, who spoke of this legislation as a weapon which was to be used to compel an agreement by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. But while we are all more than pleased with the conciliatory words of the Minister of Public Works, I want to put it to him and to the House: What is going to happen to the people of the Prairie Provinces and of British Columbia, who depend on the Grand Trunk Pacific railway facilities in these provinces, if and when the Government act under the authority they now take?

Do you think any
government would be allowed to stay in power ten minutes which would not take all the freight that was offered at Winnipeg, and all the freight offered by the Grand Trunk in the East, and move it over that line. The trouble about operating that line will be to get enough freight for it. There is no government that would be foolish enough to attempt for a minute any other policy.

The hon. member has
more faith in governments than I have.
He has more reason to.
The hon. member has more experience than I have had.

That may be the reason, but I must say that the experience we have had at the hands of this Government would not lead to his conclusion by any means. If we are to have so much faith in the

Government which is going to use this legislation as a weapon against the company, how sure are we that the Government will not continue to use this control of the traffic conditions as a weapon also to compel some other concession. We are not interested in the Grand Trunk Pacific, but we are interested in the people of the West; we are interested in their getting railway facilities and under the best possible circumstances. We are interested in the maintenance of effective railway competition, and certainly we look with very great disfavour upon a condition of affairs that will cut off from the thousands of miles of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway in those Prairie Provinces access to lake navigation on their own lines under their own conditions. As a western man, I would certainly, under those circumstances, seeing that we have the competition of two other roads from the prairies to the lakes, rather trust the Grand Trunk Pacific than this Government. I will not suggest this, but I think it will suggest itself to the minds of a great many people that, if this Government has friends among the railway system of Canada, and if it should be particularly well-disposed towards one or the other or both of the other railway systems in the West, it would be a very easy matter for the Government so to handle its control of this connection between lake Superior and Winnipeg to throw the traffic to those other systems. Who thinks the Government would not do that? I certainly do not, and I think there are very few people in the Northwest who would believe the Government would not do it.
Would it not be time to complain when the Government does it?

No, it would be too late
then. I am putting my protest in here and now, at the time when the Government is asking for the authority and power. If the Government takes that power, it takes it in the face of the -naming that I have given, and it will certa: uly have to account to the people in the Northwest for the action it proposes to take.
Is not this section from Winnipeg to lake Superior Junction still in the hands of the Government?
Yes.
Until that section is taken over by the Grand Trunk Pacific, they cannot run over their own line to lake Superior.
No.

Therefore the piece of
road from Winnipeg to lake Superior is practically valueless to the Grand Trunk Pacific until they get their lease. Until such time as they complete the contract, they are certainly in no better position than they will be if the Government keeps control of it.

That is perfectly true. The Government owns the line from Winnipeg to lake Superior Junction, and the Government can to-day cut the Grand Trunk Pacific off from the operation of that line when the temporary lease that they have at present runs out.
They want to give it up now.
I have very grave doubts.

Grave doubts about
my statement?

About their wishing to
give it up.
I make the emphatic statement that they do wish to give it up. Now contradict my statement.

I am sorry to have been
thought to be discourteous to the minister. Certainly I did not wish to be so, and I wish to accept unqualifiedly any statement he sees fit to make. I do not wish to be thought for a moment as doubting any statement he wishes to make; but as a matter of business operation, there is no doubt that, as long as the Grand Trunk Pacific wishes to operate from Winnipeg to Lake Superior Junction, the Government will be just as ill-advised to prevent them from operating as it will be to expropriate this piece of line. It is not the details of the question about which I am worrying; it is the general question that that company, which has thousands of miles throughout the Prairie Provinces, must have the right of access to lake Superior, or they cannot carry on business on a competitive basis with their competitors, and the people of the Northwest must necessarily suffer in traffic facilities as a consequence.

If they wanted to get
access all they would require to do would be to take over the line.

They will take over the
line if this Government will complete it. The point is that the Government has not completed the line. The Government does not say that it has completed the line; but it is going to take legislation from this
Parliament which it will use as a weapon to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to take over the line without its being completed.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 119, to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
Railways and Canals-National Transcontinental railway construction, $5,000,000.

['It is 20 feet or more for the whole 15 miles.
Progress reported.

Thursday, April 1, 1915.']
What is that for?
I am not going back on my statement. We claim it is for construction, and there will be a lot of things to complete five years from now-yes, ten years from now.
Thirty years from now.
Fifty years from now.
The Solicitor General will surely be able to give us some explanation of this $5,000,000 for construction on the National- Transcontinental railway.
If the hon. gentleman does not understand it, I am afraid the case is hopeless for him.
The Solicitor General is arguing that the road was completed.
The Solicitor General has the engineers behind him.
Quite a way behind him -$5,000,000.
I have been able to quote exactly what the engineer said.
Will this $5,000,000 complete the road?
It shows the following expenditures: grading, $1,702,750-
Where?
That is paying for grading under these contracts not settled.
Work done?
Yes; right of way, $575,000.	'
Where?

Well, a portion of it in the city of Winnipeg. We have a lawsuit there. We were sued for nearly $3,000,000 by one company; went to the Exchequer Court and they got judgment for $465,000. Another item is, building, $60,000.
Building what?
The Champlain station -to finish it.
Will that be finished this year?
Oh, yes.
"Oh, yes"-I have heard that before; I heard it last year.
I know, but I tell the right hon. gentleman it will be. There is $10,000 still due on bridges. Then, Quebec terminals, $2,500,000.
What terminals?
Joint terminals with the Canadian Pacific railway. The Trans-cona shops will take $30,000, and headquarters salaries and expenses, $40,000.
If the road is completed, headquarters expenses ought to stop.
There are old disputes to which we fell heir, disputes seven, eight and nine years old, and it takes some time to straighten them out.
And do you need all these overhead expenses for that?
That is part of it. My hon. friend knows well that we have to keep some of these engineers that supervise the work if we get into a lawsuit. This totals $5,000,000.

Of this,
$2,500,000 goes to the Quebec terminals. Is that to be paid to the Canadian Pacific Railway for land?

We take the land in our own right, and enter into a terminal agreement with them on practically the same basis as that on which the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific have entered into agreement with the Canadian Northern Railway in Winnipeg.
Has the land been bought?
Most of it, and that which has not been bought has been filed upon.
Not paid for?

No. I think there is some land yet to be paid for along the shore up near the Champlain .12 m. market. And if I wanted to be critical and bring politics into this, in my opinion, we could take a good deal of credit for securing that land at so much lower price than was offered in the Exchequer Court-from Wolfe's Cove up to Champlain market. But I have avoided discussions of that kind.

And if I wanted to be critical I would condemn the whole scheme. I understood from the minister's statement that he is buying that land in the right of the Government. My impression of the contract laid on the table last session was that the land was acquired by the Canadian Pacific Railway, the station was to be built by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and we have to pay 24 per cent upon the total. If that be so, the land must be acquired by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
No, they hold a certain quantity, but we buy the balance. I can show the right hon. gentleman the plan of the scheme.
I saw the plans. Evidently my impression is wrong. Upon what is this expenditure of 24 per cent to the Canadian Pacific railway based?
We pay 24 per cent on their land. Then we have a terminal agreement on a pro rata basis. They pay 24 per cent on our land, so "it is as broad as it is long.
Do I understand the arrangement to be that we pay 24 per cent on what is owned by the Cana-* dian Pacific Railway, then we buy the adjacent land and they use it with us? What do they pay?
They have land to a certain amount, and on the value of that we pay 24 per cent. We buy land, and on the price that we pay they pay us 24 per cent.
Can the hon. gentleman tell us now when these works will be completed? Is $5,000,000 sufficient to complete the works on the line which are now incomplete?

That will depend to some extent on how the contracts finished are settled. My hon. friend knows that there have been many disputes in the

carrying out of these contracts which have never been settled. We may have to go to the Exchequer Court on many of these. If we can settle these contracts for what they claim, we shall be able to complete the road and pay these besides. The right of way through Ontario has never been settled for. There is some right of way in the province of Quebec and. some in the province of New Brunswick that is not settled yet. We have made careful estimates of what we think would be just and fair and have based our Estimates on that.
There are shops, the station, the line from the Cap Rouge region down, and yards, etc., to be completed at Quebec. Will this amount complete all of these things?
My engineer says so, but I put in the proviso that we are assuming we can settle the debts still owing on the old contracts at a fair figure. We have not done that yet.
Will the other work that we have been discussing to-night be finished this year?
Yes.
The Prime Minister, at a gathering at Quebec submitted plans for a tunnel and told them it was to be constructed. That is not included in this?
Oh, no; that will cost from a million to a million and a half dollars.
It will cost two million dollars.
Well, I know. As soon as the business of the road warrants us to going to that expense we will do it.
It is not intended this year, for what we may call the completion of these works, to include the tunnel?

No, we could not this year.
Hudson Bay railway-construction of railway, terminals and elevators, $5,500,000.

What is for the railway and what for the terminals?
IVIr. COCHRANE:	For the railway,
$4,000,000, and for the terminals, $1,500,000.
That is this year's vote?

Yes, and we have in the Supplementary Estimates a balance that we
overran our vote with the contractor for 1914-15.
What is the condition of the construction of the railway? How many miles of steel and grading, and how many miles of work has been done?

The track has been laid to mile 214 from the Pas. The grading is done to mile 293, and the contractor has made arrangements to prosecute the grading between this point and mile 390 during the coming season. There remains the completion of grading to Port Nelson, mile 424, the track-laying from mile 214, and the ballasting, steel bridges and construction of buildings.
What is the condition of the two bridges across the Nelson river?

One is now under contract, the other one is not completely worked out. The engineering difficulties have yet to be settled. They worked on the first bridge aoross the Nelson river, changed it. about and saved a lot of money.
Is the steel up to the first bridge ?
No, it is about 24 miles from it, but they are laying it very fast.
Is the grading beyond the first bridge ?
Oh yes, the bridge is to be in place by the 15th of September, so that the rails can* be laid as far as it is graded next fall, before the snow falls.
How soon is it expected that the railway will be completed to Port Nelson ?
I think 1916, but the engineer thinks we will have hard work to do it.
He is right.
In the fall of 1916 ?
Yes.
Have any special difficulties developed in the way of handling the grading work ?
No. To show you to what extent we have secured a straight line, as the crow flies the distance would be 406 miles, .and the length of the railway is 424 miles. For that distance, that is pretty good.
Would the minister make a statement in regard to the terminals ? I asked last year for a plan of the harbour improvements and the estimated cost and time for completion.

We have not the plans here. The deepwater channel, about ^ mile wide, up the middle of the estuary, is separated from the shore by wide tidal fiats over which the water is from one to three feet deep at low water. It is proposed to construct the docks parallel to the deep water channel and distant about
1,000	feet therefrom, the intervening space being dredged about 20 feet at low water. The docks will consist of a cigar-shaped area surrounded with timber cribs and filled in with dredged material. The area will be about 500 feet wide and f (three quarters) mile long, in extreme dimensions. Along the face of the docks the steamer berths will be dredged to 30 feet depth. The elevator will be situated on the above described area, with adequate trackage. The docks will be connected with the shore by a series of crib piers (of laTge area to resist ice thrust) connected up with steel spans.
They consider this better than a solid pier.
Tlhe steamer Minto has been up twice to my knowledge right opposite where this dock will be, and that without any dredging. Of course the channel will have to be straightened in some places. The Minto went up, and there were no buoys there, and she got in and out again all right.
What is the draught of the Minto?

Twenty feet. Of
course the chief difficulty is that the water from that channel in to the shore is low.
I understand there is a deep water channel a quarter of a mile wide being dredged.
No, it is a natural channel.
What is the depth of it?
The Minto has been up there and she draws twenty feet. I should not think the depth is much more than that.

Is it the intention to
dredge deeper. Ocean steamers draw thirty feet or more.

Until the route has
been approved I do not think it will
be necessary to do more than straighten 
out the channel. Of course when the route has been settled, most decidedly we shall dredge. The boats can come in there now at high tide, and even at low tide.
How much dredging has been done up to the present?

No dredging has been done. Owing to the long ocean voyage it was necessary to ship the dredge in a more or less " knocked down " condition. That is to say the heavy top hammer of "A" frame, cutterhead ladder, etc., were dismantled and stowed upon the deck. Also consideration of stowage on shipboard made it necessary to ship the pontoons and discharge pipes as separate plates and loose parts (shaped, and punched, with necessary forgings, etc., but not assembled.) It was intended that this assembly work should be done during the winter of 1913-14, so that dredge could be put at work during the summer of 1914. Owing to late arrival at the Bay, desertion of labour and loss of necessary tools in the ship wrecks, this work could not be proceeded with to advantage until the steamers arrived last September, and was not sufficiently advanced to permit of actual ivork before the close of river operations in the middle of October. The dredge was however tested and the machinery found to be in good working order. She was very late in getting in there last year. She started on July 3, but did not get in until August 14. This year we have our men and plant up there, and hope to make considerable progress.
Just how much dredging is it intended to do in order to reach deep water?
For about 1,000 feet wide, and the length of the dock, which will be about half a mile.
The Government is undertaking now to dredge and straighten out the channel to deep water.
We shall not do the dredging till the last. There will be no trouble in the boats getting in there. A boat drawing twenty feet can get in all right.
You were rather unfortunate the season before last in the arrival of vessels. How was it last year?

I do not think we
were to blame in any sense of the word. We were unfortunate in not having enough lighters up there. I am satisfied that both

those boats that were lost were deliberately stranded. That is a strong statement to make, but I am sure I am right.
How many vessels went up?
There were 37 passages through the Strait this last summer, notwithstanding the late season. By passages, I mean going and coming.

The first passage was
through at what time?
The first steamer got to Port Nelson on August 14.
How does that compare with the year before?
It was eight days later.
Is it a fact that it was not usual for vessels to get there before the beginning of August?

We have been late two years, but I do not blame the route for that. Of course the great difficulty is when you have ice and fog together. With wireless telegraphy there is no danger from one of these conditions alone, as the boats can keep in touch with one another. The shores are high, and there is deep water right up to the shores. We found it paid last year to buy two sailing ships and load them with coal in England and bring them over. We delivered the coal and paid for the ships at a less cost than we could have taken the coal up. These ships had the largest draft of any of the boats up there-22 feet.
Those boats got in?
They were towed in. The boats anchored just a little way out, and the coal was taken out of them and used on our own boats in the channel.
You brought it up to where the port is likely to be?
Yes. .
How many miles of deep water are there inside of what you would call the port, that is, in the mouth of the river?
Fifteen miles.

Does that 20 feet depth
hold for that distance?
It would be more than that in some cases, but you can count on 20. Of course, if a boat with a 30-foot draft waited for high tide she could get in.
At Fort William there is a stretch of water seven or eight miles long and the water remains deep.
That was dredged.
It was originally pretty deep. Does the 20-foot depth hold for the 15 miles up at Port Nelson?

It is 20 feet or more for the whole 15 miles.
